ordered_diagnoses: Bile duct stricture due to chemotherapy

s1.syndrome_frame: Cholestatic jaundice with bile duct strictures and dilatations in a patient with a history of chemotherapy
salient_findings: Wall thickening of the extrahepatic and intrahepatic bile ducts and of the gallbladder
key_facts: 61-year-old woman with cervical cancer
Metastatic to paraaortic and left supraclavicular lymph nodes
Treated with paclitaxel for 63 days
Treated with bevacizumab for 36 days
Treated with cisplatin
Admitted for marked elevation of liver enzymes
AST 173 U/L
ALT 221 U/L
γ-GTP 2553 U/L
ALP 5188 U/L
Abdominal ultrasonography showed wall thickening of the bile ducts and gallbladder
Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed wall thickening of the bile ducts with luminal narrowing and dilation
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with sphincterotomy and nasobiliary drainage was performed
Biopsy of the common bile duct showed no malignant cells
Bile cytology was negative for malignancy
Ursodeoxycholic acid was started on day 6

shortlist: Bile duct stricture due to chemotherapy

shortlist.label: Primary sclerosing cholangitis
shortlist.why_kept: Cholestatic jaundice with bile duct strictures and dilatations

shortlist.label: Bile duct stricture due to chemotherapy
shortlist.why_kept: History of chemotherapy with paclitaxel, bevacizumab, and cisplatin

shortlist.label: IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis
shortlist.why_kept: Inflammatory condition causing bile duct strictures and dilatations

shortlist.label: Cholangiocarcinoma
shortlist.why_kept: Malignant condition causing bile duct strictures and dilatations, although biopsy was negative

shortlist.label: Sclerosing cholangitis due to paclitaxel
shortlist.why_kept: Specific chemotherapy agent associated with bile duct injury

raw.rationale: The patient's recent treatment with paclitaxel for 63 days, followed by the development of marked elevation of liver enzymes and bile duct changes, suggests a drug-induced cause. The absence of malignant cells in the biopsy and negative bile cytology make cholangiocarcinoma less likely. The patient's clinical presentation and temporal relationship with paclitaxel treatment support sclerosing cholangitis due to paclitaxel as the most plausible diagnosis.
